title: Why Getting into System Design Is Probably the Best Decision
content:
I spent a long time building applications without ever asking how the things underneath them actually worked. I could ship a FastAPI service, put Postgres behind it, throw Redis in front of it, and call it a day. It worked. It also would have fallen over the second anything interesting happened to it, and I would not have known why.
Getting into system design changed that, and honestly it might be the best technical decision I have made so far. Not because it handed me a list of architectures to memorize, but because it changed the questions I ask before I write any code.
## What "purely distributed" actually means
A lot of people use "distributed" to mean "it runs on more than one machine." That is not really it. You can run one app across twenty machines and still have a system that dies the moment one specific box goes down.
A system is purely distributed when no single machine is load bearing. Any node can disappear and the system keeps answering correctly. Not "keeps answering," which is easy. Keeps answering correctly, which is the hard part.
That distinction is the whole game. Once you accept that any node can die at any moment, everything else follows. You cannot keep important state in one process's memory. You cannot have a single writer that everyone waits on. You cannot assume a message that was sent was received. Every design decision after that is downstream of treating failure as normal rather than exceptional.
## Stateless and stateful, and why the line keeps moving
The first real unlock for me was understanding stateless versus stateful properly, rather than as a vocabulary word.
A stateless service does not remember anything about you between requests. Everything it needs arrives with the request. That sounds like a limitation until you notice what it buys you: every replica is interchangeable. If you are running ten copies, it does not matter which one your request hits. If one dies mid request, the retry lands somewhere else and works fine. You scale it by adding boxes. There is no coordination cost, because there is nothing to coordinate.
A stateful service is the opposite. It remembers. A database remembers rows, a queue remembers position, a stream processor remembers windows. That memory is the thing that makes it useful and also the thing that makes it hard, because now the identity of the machine matters. You cannot just add a box and have it help. The new box has no idea what happened before it showed up.
The evolution of most real systems is basically a long project of pushing state out of the places where holding it is expensive and into the smaller number of places where you are willing to pay for it. Sessions move out of app memory and into a token or a shared cache. Uploads move off local disk and into object storage. Business logic gets rewritten so it takes an ID and looks things up instead of holding onto an object across calls.
You are not eliminating state. State has to live somewhere. You are concentrating it, so the layer that has to be careful stays as small as possible and the layer that has to be enormous does not have to be careful at all.
## The part where a million people press the same button
Here is what finally made system design click for me.
When you push far enough on that separation, you end up with a stateless tier that can grow essentially without limit. A million people can hit the same endpoint at the same instant and it does not care, because none of those requests know about each other. Add machines, add capacity, done. If a machine dies in the middle of it, a few requests retry and nobody notices.
But the problem does not go away. It relocates. Everything you took out of the stateless tier landed in the stateful tier, and now you have a million concurrent operations converging on the systems that actually have to remember things. That is where the interesting engineering lives: partitioning so that not every write lands in the same place, replication so that losing a node does not lose data, consensus so the replicas agree on what happened and in what order.
Fault tolerance at that scale is not a feature you add at the end. It is a consequence of the shape. The stateless tier survives failure because its parts are disposable. The stateful tier survives failure because its parts are replicated and can elect a new leader when one falls over. Neither of those is something you bolt on later.
## Consistency or availability, and being honest about which one you picked
The other thing system design does to your brain is force you to actually choose.
When the network splits and two halves of your cluster cannot talk to each other, you get exactly one choice. Keep serving and risk handing out stale or conflicting answers, or refuse to serve until you can be sure you are right. You do not get both. There is no clever implementation that sneaks around it.
What surprised me is how often the right answer is consistency, and how often the default ends up being availability without anybody having decided that. If two people buy the last ticket, or a balance goes negative, or an inventory count drifts, "at least it stayed up" is not a comfort. Being unavailable for four seconds is a much better outcome than being wrong forever.
Plenty of the time it goes the other way, of course. A like counter, a view count, a recommendation feed: those can be a little stale and nobody is harmed. The point is not that one answer is correct. The point is that it is a decision, made per feature, and if you have not made it deliberately then you have made it by accident.
That is the mindset shift. You stop asking "how do I build this" and start asking "what is this allowed to get wrong, and for how long."
## What I have actually been learning
Most of this has come from watching Jordan Has No Life on YouTube. I have gone through a lot of his system design content over the past few months and it is the first material that made distributed systems feel like engineering with reasons behind it, rather than a set of diagrams to memorize. He spends his time on the tradeoffs instead of the buzzwords, which is exactly what I needed.
The part that pulled me in furthest is indexing, because it is where the abstract stuff turns into bytes on disk.
I started with hash indexes. The idea is about as simple as it gets: keep a hash map in memory from key to the byte offset where that key's value lives in a file on disk. Look up a key, get an offset, seek, read. Point lookups are roughly constant time, and writes are just appends, which is fast precisely because you never seek in order to write.
Then you hit the limits, and the limits are what teach you. The entire key space has to fit in memory, because the hash map is the index. Range queries are impossible, because a hash function deliberately destroys ordering, so "give me every key between A and F" means scanning everything. And because you are appending, the same key ends up written many times over and you need compaction to reclaim the space.
So now I am working through B-tree indexing, and the tradeoffs invert almost exactly. A B-tree keeps keys sorted, which is the entire point of it. Range scans become cheap, ordered iteration is natural, and the index lives on disk in fixed size pages instead of having to fit in RAM. Lookups become logarithmic instead of constant. Writes get more expensive, because you are modifying pages in place and occasionally splitting them, which is also why B-trees need a write ahead log to survive a crash in the middle of a split.
Neither one is better. A hash index is better at exactly one thing, and a B-tree is better at almost everything else while being slower at that one thing. Every real database picks based on what it expects people to ask it.
## Next up: Udahe database
The plan after writing this is to go back to my database project, Udahe database, and actually implement this in Rust instead of just understanding it.
Reading about a B-tree and writing a B-tree are not the same activity, and I have found that out the hard way more than once. You do not really know what a page split costs until you have to handle a node filling up mid insert. You do not really understand write ahead logging until you have killed the process at a bad moment and had to recover from whatever happened to be on disk.
So the goal is to build the indexing layer for real, and then start moving toward the distributed side: replication, then leader election, then deciding where I want to sit on the consistency question and being able to defend it.
## Why students should care about this earlier than they think
If you are a student moving from finishing assignments to actually building applications, this is the highest leverage thing you can study.
Not because you are going to design something at Google scale next semester. You are not, and that is fine. It is because system design gives you the vocabulary for the questions that decide whether what you build survives contact with reality. Where does state live. What happens when this node dies. What are we allowed to get wrong. How does this fail, and does it fail loudly or quietly.
Before I learned any of this, my instinct with a new project was to open an editor. Now my instinct is to work out what the data looks like, who writes it, who reads it, what has to be correct and what can be approximate, and only then start typing. The code ends up simpler, because most of the complexity in a bad design comes from decisions you did not know you were making.
You do not need to have built a distributed system to think this way. You just need to know the questions exist. That alone is worth it.
preview: What "purely distributed" actually means, how systems evolve from stateful to stateless until a million people can press the same button at once, and what hash indexes and B-trees have been teaching me along the way.

title: I Failed My Classes. It Was the Best Thing That Ever Happened to Me.
content:
There was a version of me from last semester who would have never let that title exist.
That version had a 3.9 GPA, never missed an assignment, was grinding research, holding down a part-time internship, and trying to build a startup on the side. I wore the chaos like a badge of honor. I thought I was built different, some kind of academic weapon who didn't have to choose.
Something had to give.
This semester, it was my grades.
I had to take a W on one class. And it looks like I'm not going to pass another. A few months ago, that sentence would have broken me. But here's the thing: I'm not sad about it. I'm genuinely grateful.
Because failing taught me something that a 4.0 never could: I'm not a superhero. I'm a human. And humans have limits.
For so long I thought time management meant doing everything, just faster, just harder. What I actually needed to learn was how to prioritize. Not every class, every assignment, every opportunity deserves the same version of you. And when you try to give 100% to eight things at once, you're really giving 12% to everything.
Letting go of the academic perfectionism didn't break me. It freed me.
Right now I'm happier than I've ever been. I just got back from Japan. My internship at Liberty kicks off in about a month, and I'm meeting my manager on Thursday, and I'm excited, not anxious, not burned out. Just genuinely excited.
The startup work feels more focused. The things I'm building actually mean something to me now, because I chose them over other things. That choice has weight to it.
If you're a student trying to do it all (the grades, the internship, the side project, the research), I'm not going to tell you to quit. I'm just going to tell you: pick your thing. Go all in on it. And don't be afraid of what you have to let go of to get there.
Failure isn't the end of the story. Sometimes it's just the plot twist that finally points you in the right direction.
preview: How losing my GPA helped me find my priorities, and why I've never been happier.

title: What Japan Taught Me About Systems Thinking
content:
I just got back from Japan. And I came home a better engineer, not because I was coding the whole time, but because I wasn't.
Japan has this reputation for being intense. Work hard, be disciplined, respect the process. And that's all true. But what actually hit me wasn't the work ethic. It was the design of everything around it. The way the culture balances intensity with rest, individuality with collective consideration. The way the whole country, from its transit systems to its convenience stores, just... works.
That's when it clicked for me: Japan isn't just a culture. It's an architecture.

Every System Has a Contract
One of the first things you notice in Japan is how considerate everything is, not in a soft, passive way, but in a deeply intentional way. Quiet train cars. Designated smoking areas. Trash cans that only exist in specific places, yet somehow the streets are spotless.
This isn't compliance. It's a social API.
Everyone operates with an implicit understanding of their role within the larger system. You don't need a sign saying "be quiet". The contract is understood. Each component trusts the others to hold up their end of the interface.
In software, we call this a well-defined boundary. The best-architected systems aren't the ones with the most enforcement. They're the ones where every service knows exactly what it's responsible for, and nothing more. Tight contracts. Minimal surface area. No one bleeds into someone else's domain.
When your components are that well-defined, the system becomes predictable. And predictable systems are fast systems.

Work Hard, Play Hard, and Why That's Actually a Systems Principle
There's a concept in Japan called ikigai: roughly, your reason for being. Your purpose. And what strikes me about Japanese work culture isn't just the discipline, it's the intentionality. Work is work. Rest is rest. There's a reason izakayas are packed on Friday nights. People actually decompress. They switch contexts completely.
Software engineers talk about context-switching as a tax. And it is. But there's a deeper systems concept here: isolation.
The most resilient architectures are the ones where failure in one domain doesn't cascade into another. A database going down shouldn't take out your entire application. A bad deploy in one service shouldn't corrupt another. You build walls not because you distrust your components, but because you respect the integrity of each one.
The Japanese version of work-hard-play-hard isn't sloppy context-switching. It's true isolation. When you're working, you're fully in that context. When you're off, you're fully off. No half-states. No undefined behavior.
Engineers who can't truly rest are engineers running without garbage collection. Eventually, memory leaks.

Kaizen: The Feedback Loop as a First-Class Citizen
You can't talk about Japan and engineering without talking about kaizen: continuous improvement. It's the philosophy behind Toyota's production system, and it's been borrowed by every agile framework since. But most engineers treat kaizen like a retro buzzword.
The real insight is architectural: feedback loops should be first-class citizens in your system design, not afterthoughts.
Most systems are built to do things. Fewer are built to learn things. But the systems that scale, the ones that survive, are the ones that can observe themselves, catch their own drift, and self-correct. Observability isn't a DevOps checkbox. It's the difference between a system that degrades silently and one that tells you it's struggling before it falls over.
Japan's infrastructure doesn't just run well because it was built well. It runs well because the feedback loops (maintenance schedules, civic reporting, cultural norms) are baked into how the system operates. Improvement isn't a sprint. It's a property of the system itself.

Bring It Back
I came back from Japan not with a list of tourist highlights, but with a mental model I keep returning to:
The best systems, cultural or technical, are the ones where every component knows its contract, isolates its state, and participates in its own improvement.

{{img:images/posts/1773088569099.jpeg}}

That's not a Japanese idea. That's just good architecture. But sometimes it takes stepping inside a system that actually works to finally see it clearly.
Now I'm back. Building. And I'm thinking about my systems a little differently
preview: The country runs like a well-architected system. Once you see it, you can't unsee it.

title: I Go to a School You've Never Heard Of. I Still Got Interviews at Bloomberg, Capital One, HubSpot, NVIDIA, Jane Street, Liberty Mutual Lockheed Martin and way more
content:
I'm a sophomore. My university doesn't have a target school pipeline. No recruiters camping out at our career fair. No alumni network feeding into Wall Street or Silicon Valley. If you Googled my school, you'd probably move on in three seconds.
And yet: Bloomberg. Capital One. HubSpot. NVIDIA. Jane Street. Liberty Mutual. Lockheed Martin.
I'm not saying this to flex. I'm saying this because when I was a freshman, I genuinely believed the school you attended determined the opportunities you could access. I was wrong. And I want to be specific about why, because "believe in yourself" is not advice.

What Actually Moved the Needle
1. My GitHub Was My Real Resume
Recruiters at big companies see thousands of resumes. Most of them are identical: same bullet points, same buzzwords, same GPA padding. What they don't see every day is a sophomore with a GitHub that actually shows them you can build things.
I stopped treating projects as resume fillers and started treating them as products. Every repo had a README that explained the why, not just the what. Screenshots. Architecture diagrams. Deployment links where I could manage it. I wanted anyone who landed on my profile to understand what I built and why it mattered in under 60 seconds.
Your GitHub is a portfolio. Treat it like one.
2. Startup Experience Signals Things a GPA Can't
Before any of these interviews, I was already working on a startup. Unpaid. Nights and weekends. And I'll be honest: there were moments I questioned whether it was worth it.
It was worth it.
Not because of the equity, not because it's going to make me rich, but because it gave me stories that GPA kids can't tell. I could talk about making real architectural decisions with no senior engineer holding my hand. I could talk about shipping features to actual users and watching them use it. I could talk about what happens when something breaks in production and it's just you.
That is rocket fuel in a technical interview. Senior engineers don't want to babysit someone who only knows how to pass tests. They want someone who has felt the pressure of real stakes and kept building anyway.
3. LeetCode, But With Intention
I'm not going to pretend grinding LeetCode isn't part of the game. It is. But there's a version of LeetCode grinding that prepares you for interviews and a version that just racks up solved problems without understanding.
I focused on pattern recognition over volume. Once you truly understand sliding window, you don't need to memorize thirty sliding window problems. You need to see the shape of the problem and know which tool to reach for. I drilled the fundamentals hard: trees, graphs, dynamic programming, recursion. And I practiced explaining my thinking out loud, because the algorithm is only half of what they're evaluating.
Communicate your thought process. Always.

The Honest Truth About Unknown Schools
Here's what I've come to believe: prestige is a shortcut for lazy evaluation. When a recruiter sees MIT on a resume, they skip a few mental steps. When they see a school they don't recognize, you have to do that work yourself, upfront, through your projects, your experience, your presence online.
That's not unfair. That's just the game. And once you understand the game, you can play it.
The students getting filtered out from unknown schools aren't getting filtered out because they're less capable. They're getting filtered out because they're playing by rules that were written for a different type of candidate. Build in public. Put your work where people can find it. Make it impossible to ignore you.

A Note on Unpaid Startup Work
I get asked about this a lot. Is it worth working for a startup for free?
My answer: it depends on what you're getting paid in.
If you're getting paid in real responsibility, real ownership, and real learning, that has a dollar value that some paid internships can't match. I learned more from six months of unpaid startup work than I did from coursework in the same period. I made decisions that mattered. I shipped code that real people used. I failed fast and fixed faster.
But be honest with yourself about what you're actually getting. If you're doing grunt work for someone's half-baked idea with no equity, no mentorship, and no autonomy, that's not an investment. That's just free labor. Ask yourself: will this make me better? Will I have a story to tell because of this?
If the answer is yes, do it. The compounding on real experience is insane.
If the answer is no, walk.

You Don't Need Permission
No one is going to recruit you out of obscurity. No one is going to find your potential and hand you an opportunity because you have a good heart and work hard. You have to put the work somewhere visible, tell a story with it, and go get the thing you want.
Your school is not your story. What you build is.

title: The AI Paper That Changed How We Build Docere
content:
{{img:images/posts/download.png}}

A few months ago, a paper came across my feed that made me stop everything I was doing.
The Darwin Gödel Machine, published at ICLR 2026, describes a system that does something most AI researchers said was years away: an agent that rewrites its own code, tests each modification against a real benchmark, and keeps an archive of every variant that improved performance. Darwinian selection, applied to agent design itself.
The result was a coding agent that improved its own SWE-bench score from 20% to 50%, autonomously. No human intervention. No retraining. Just a loop: try something, measure it, keep what works.
I read that and immediately thought about classrooms.

The problem with every AI tutor on the market
ChatGPT is the same tutor today as it was a year ago. So is Khanmigo. So is every AI tutor I've seen.
They don't get better at teaching. They get better at sounding like they're teaching, through prompt engineering, RLHF, model upgrades. But none of them close the loop. None of them ask the only question that matters:
Did the student actually learn?
That question haunts me. I've spent two years building Docere, an AI tutoring platform deployed in two Minnesota middle schools with 500+ students. I've sat in classrooms. I've watched students interact with AI. And the thing that kept bothering me was this:
We had no way of knowing if our tutoring strategies were actually working. Not in a "the student said they understood" way, but in a "their grades went up and they retained the material three weeks later" way.
The DGM paper gave us a framework to solve that.

What "benchmark" means in education
In the original paper, the benchmark is SWE-bench, a set of coding tasks with clear pass/fail criteria. The agent modifies itself, runs the benchmark, and measures the delta. Simple.
Education doesn't have that. Or at least, people assume it doesn't.
But we realized something: if your AI tutor is connected to a real Learning Management System (and ours is, through direct integrations with Canvas, Moodle, Blackboard), then you do have a benchmark. You have quiz scores. Assignment grades. Engagement data. Submission patterns. You have real, measurable outcomes tied to real students in real courses.
The question becomes: can you trace those outcomes back to the specific tutoring interactions that preceded them?
At Docere, the answer is yes. We've been building toward this for over 40 weeks.

A tutor that teaches itself to teach
I won't get into the full technical architecture, since we have a research paper in progress for AIED 2026 in Seoul that will cover that properly. But here's the idea at a high level:
Docere doesn't use one fixed tutoring approach. It maintains a population of teaching strategies. Each strategy represents a different way of guiding a student through a concept: different questioning techniques, different levels of scaffolding, different ways of connecting new material to what the student already knows.
After every tutoring session, the system evaluates: did this interaction move the needle? Not "did the student say they understood", but did their actual performance improve?
Strategies that consistently lead to better outcomes get prioritized. Strategies that don't get phased out. And new variations get introduced, tested, and either kept or discarded.
Over time, the tutor gets better. Not because we shipped a new prompt. Because the system figured out what works, for different students, in different subjects, at different levels.
That's the part that gets me excited. This isn't a static product. It's a system that compounds.

Why this matters beyond Docere
The DGM paper is about coding agents, but the principle is universal: any AI system with access to a reliable feedback signal can improve itself through selection.
In education, that feedback signal has always existed. It's called a grade. We just never connected it to the AI doing the teaching.
I think this is where the entire AI-in-education space is headed. Not bigger models. Not better prompts. Closed-loop systems that measure what matters and evolve based on evidence.
We're not the only ones who will figure this out. But right now, with 500+ students, 10,000+ memories captured, and a research paper in progress, we might be the furthest along.
If you're interested in self-improving AI systems, education technology, or the intersection of the two, I'd love to hear from you. We're presenting at AIED 2026 in Seoul this summer, and we're always looking for collaborators, researchers, and people who think the future of education should be built on evidence, not vibes.
Youdahe
preview: How a self-improving coding agent inspired a self-improving tutor.

title: I thought about github before tom preston
content:
I need to come clean about something.
Before I was born, I was a ghost.
Not like a scary ghost. More like a little floating idea ghost, drifting through the universe, just vibing. Collecting concepts. Putting them in my invisible pockets for no reason whatsoever.
And one day I floated past Tom Preston Werner while he was thinking really hard about something and I HEARD IT. The whole idea. Version control. Repositories. The whole thing.
But here is the deal. I thought of it first. By like half a second. Maybe a full second. I was a very quick ghost.
Except my version was not for code.
My version was for SOUP.
What if your grandma made a terrible batch of chili and needed to roll back to the previous commit. What if there were BRANCHES of the same stew. What if two aunts could open a PULL REQUEST on grandmas secret jambalaya and she could review it and leave comments like "this cilantro suggestion is not ready for production."
I tried to file a patent. As a ghost. As a prenatal soup-versioning specter floating around in 2005.
The patent office rejected me. No address. No social security number. No body.
Then I got born in 2006 and forgot everything instantly like a Windows XP crash with no recovery file.
Tom shipped in 2008.
Suspicious. Very suspicious.{{img:images/posts/351d11dee112d732ad82699e1b2adb48.jpg}}

title: First Week at Liberty Mutual: Initial Impressions
content:
Wrapping up my first week at Liberty Mutual, I can already say it has been a really interesting start. Coming in, I had a certain expectation of what working at an insurance company would look like, but I have been genuinely surprised by how much it feels like a financial infrastructure company at its core.

There is a strong focus on systems, data, and how information moves through the organization. That gives everything a more technical and analytical edge than I expected. It is not just about policies and claims. It is about the underlying frameworks that make all of that possible at scale.
I am still getting ramped up, but the project I am working on lowkey feels like the perfect fit. It is something that is honestly a bit above my current understanding, which I actually really like. It gives me a solid benchmark to see how fast I can learn and grow. It is challenging in a good way and keeps me on my toes.

One of the highlights so far has definitely been the team. Everyone has been super welcoming and supportive, which made it easy to get comfortable quickly. There is a real sense of collaboration that makes a big difference.

Outside of work, I also got the chance to see the Hampton houses, and man these mfs are rich rich, like holy sh*t. Definitely a wild contrast and a reminder of how much money moves around in the spaces connected to this industry.

Overall, it has been a great first week, and I am excited to keep learning, keep pushing myself, and see where this experience goes.

title: carb maxxing might be the method
content:
i've been every size. 250 lbs, 140 lbs, and everywhere in between. i've done the cuts, i've done the bulks, i've tried basically every approach you can think of. and the one thing that consistently made everything worse every single time was cutting carbs.

workouts felt awful. energy was gone by the second set. i was grinding through sessions that should've felt good and just coming out feeling like trash. i thought that was just what cutting felt like. turns out i was wrong.

how i found out about carb maxxing
my friend brought it up a few weeks ago. he's been doing it for a while and kept telling me to just try it. i was skeptical  i'd been in the "carbs make you fat" headspace for a long time. but i figured i'd give it a shot.

the idea is pretty simple: keep carbs high, especially around training. your body runs on glucose. when you train, that's what it's pulling from. if you're depleted going into a session, you're working against yourself from the jump.

what actually happened
i'm not gonna sit here and say it's been some wild transformation. but lowkey my workouts have been noticeably better. i'm getting through sessions without hitting a wall. i'm not dragging myself to finish sets. the energy is just there in a way it wasn't before when i was keeping carbs low.

i always thought the sluggish feeling mid-cut was just part of the deal. like you're eating less so you feel worse, that's the trade. but i think it was specifically the low carb thing messing with my performance. calories were down but carbs were what was killing my training.

why i think low carb during a cut is actually bad
when you're already in a deficit, your body doesn't have a ton to work with. if you also tank your carbs, you're taking away the main fuel source for high-intensity work. your performance drops, your sessions get worse, and you lose the stimulus that was keeping muscle on in the first place. it kind of defeats the purpose.

keeping carbs up means you can still train hard even while eating less overall. you're not sacrificing performance to hit a number on the scale. and when training stays solid, the cut goes a lot better.

where i'm at now
i'm still figuring it out and i'm not claiming to have it all dialed in. but if you've been cutting carbs and wondering why everything feels so bad, it might just be that. try keeping them in, especially on training days, and see what happens. worked for me so far.

title: The One-Gate Problem in the Darwin Gödel Machine
content:
Last week I implemented the Darwin Gödel Machine for a startup. Not read about it, not prototyped a toy version. Took the actual paper (Zhang, Hu, Lu, Lange, Clune) and built a working version of the loop against a real production system in about a week. Somewhere in that week I found a hole in the original design, and closing it turned out to be the whole story.

Quick recap on the mechanism, since it matters for what comes next. The DGM keeps an archive of agents. Each iteration, it samples a parent from the archive, has a foundation model read that parent's own evaluation logs, propose a modification to itself, and apply that modification to produce a child. The child gets evaluated on a coding benchmark, SWE-bench or Polyglot. If the child compiles, still has the ability to edit code, and scores well enough, it gets added to the archive and becomes eligible to be sampled as a parent for the next round.

What made me actually sit with the paper instead of skimming it was the archive itself. This isn't hill-climbing. A naive self-improvement loop keeps exactly one lineage: mutate the current best, keep it if it's better, discard it if it isn't. That gets stuck in local optima constantly, because the only agent allowed to reproduce is whichever one currently holds the top score. The DGM samples parents from anywhere in the archive, weighted toward performance and novelty, not just the frontier. That's what they mean by open-endedness: the archive forms a growing tree, and the system can branch off an agent from ten generations back if that lineage has unexplored potential, instead of being locked into whatever path the most recent winner happened to take. It's the same reason genetic algorithms outperform greedy search on rugged fitness landscapes, just applied to an LLM editing its own source.

The self-referential part is the detail that actually earns the "Gödel machine" in the name. The system isn't just getting better at the target benchmark. It's improving its own ability to self-modify, because a better self-modifier produces better children, which get sampled more, which compounds. The paper reports the agent discovering things like better code editing tools, long-context window management, and a peer-review step for its own proposed diffs, none of which were hand-designed into the system. Those emerged because an agent that happened to be better at editing code was also better at editing the code that edits code.

The evaluation strategy is the part that made me trust the numbers. Full SWE-bench evaluation is expensive, so they gate it behind cheaper filters: a candidate first has to prove basic functionality on 10 tasks, then 50. Only if it clears a 40% success threshold on a 60-task subset (a cutoff explicitly chosen based on the noise they observed in preliminary runs, not an arbitrary round number) and ranks in the top two of the archive does it earn a full 200-task evaluation. It's a statistical-confidence-vs-compute-budget tradeoff, and the fact that they tuned the gate to observed noise rather than picking something clean is the kind of detail that tells you the team actually ran this thing enough times to know where it lies to you.

Their generalization check is a cross-benchmark transfer test, run after training: take the best agent discovered on SWE-bench and evaluate it cold on Polyglot, and vice versa. 28.9% and 24.5% respectively, real transfer, not benchmark-specific memorization. But notice when that check happens: after the fact, on the single best agent, not as a gate inside the loop. Nothing stops an individual mutation from overfitting its way into the archive along the way. The only acceptance criterion during evolution is functional correctness plus benchmark score. That's one gate.

For a coding agent working against SWE-bench, one gate is a reasonable tradeoff. The benchmark is large and diverse enough that gaming it without actually getting better at the underlying skill is nearly as hard as just getting better. I wasn't building a coding agent. I was building a prompt optimizer, and that changes the risk profile completely.

If the thing being mutated is a prompt, and the thing scoring it is a fixed, visible eval set, a single benchmark-score gate doesn't just risk overfitting. It invites it. An LLM asked to propose a modification that improves the score against a fixed set of examples will, given enough iterations, find the shortest path to a higher number. Sometimes that's a genuinely better prompt. Sometimes it's a prompt that's quietly memorized the shape of the eval set and would fall apart on anything slightly different. A single-gate DGM has no way to tell these apart, because it never checks anything except the number it's already optimizing against.

So I built two gates instead of one.

The first gate is our own in-house benchmark, not the one the mutation is being directly optimized against. This is the proprietary piece (I can't get into the specifics of what it measures), but the point is structural: the scoring signal driving the archive isn't the same signal I ultimately care about. That mismatch is intentional. A mutation has to move the number that matters to the business, not just the number it's staring at.

The second gate is a held-out check, run after a candidate clears the first. The mutated prompt gets evaluated against a set of examples it never saw during the mutation-and-score loop, functionally the same idea as the DGM paper's cross-benchmark transfer test, except mine runs on every candidate during evolution instead of once, after the fact, on the eventual winner. If a mutation cleared gate one by actually finding a better prompt, the held-out score should track closely with the training-time score. If it cleared gate one by overfitting, the held-out score collapses, and the mutation gets thrown out regardless of how good its original number looked.

Here's what that looked like in practice. The starting prompt scored 72 on our internal benchmark. After running the two-gate loop, the best surviving mutation scored 89, a real, substantial jump and exactly the kind of number that would make you suspicious if you'd read the DGM paper's own warnings about optimizing solely for a target metric. So I ran it against the held-out set, the data it had never been scored against during the loop.

88.

A one-point gap between the training-time score and the held-out score is not what overfitting looks like. Overfitting looks like a 30-point drop, the mutation falling apart the moment the eval set changes shape. An 89 that holds at 88 on unseen data means the mutation found something structurally better about the prompt, not something specific to the examples it was graded against.

{{img:images/posts/dgm-notebook.jpeg}}

The original DGM's single gate makes sense for the problem it was built to solve. The moment you point the same architecture at something narrower and more gameable than "the entire practice of software engineering" (a prompt, a scoring rubric, anything with a smaller surface area), one gate stops being a design choice and starts being a vulnerability. Two gates, one for what you actually care about and one for whether the win is real, is the fix.

Next step is figuring out whether the second gate needs to rotate. Right now the held-out set is fixed, which means a mutation could in theory start overfitting to it too, given enough generations. The DGM paper's own answer to a related problem, human review of the archive lineage, might be the honest fallback if that starts happening: not a third automated gate, just a periodic check on whether the archive is drifting somewhere the held-out set can't catch.

The other open question is whether this generalizes past prompts. Anything with a narrow, gameable scoring surface, a rubric, a classifier, a reward model, has the same one-gate vulnerability the original paper does. Worth trying on the next thing that isn't a prompt.
preview: The original DGM only checks if a mutation scores higher. That's not enough when the thing mutating is a prompt.

title: Always Being Ahead (and What to Do Instead)
content:
For most of the last two years, my life ran on a simple assumption: if I wasn't preparing for what came next, I was falling behind. Every open tab was a deadline. Every slow month felt like proof I wasn't doing enough. I called it ambition. Looking back, a lot of it was imposter syndrome wearing ambition's clothes.
The imposter syndrome didn't show up as "I'm not good enough." It showed up as motion. If I kept applying, kept interviewing, kept collecting internships and titles and processes to point to, I didn't have to sit with the quieter question underneath all of it: was I actually getting better at the thing I said I cared about, which was engineering?
For a long time the answer to that question mattered less than having an answer to a different one: am I keeping up. I looked at people further along than me and tried to become a version of them. Chase the same internship. Interview at the same companies. Follow the same "path" I saw other people posting about. I told myself this was strategy. It was actually just borrowing someone else's definition of progress because I didn't trust my own.
The problem with chasing someone else's shape is that it never ends. You land the internship and there's a better one. You get the interview and there's a more prestigious name on the list. You clear one process and there's another process waiting right behind it, asking you to prove yourself again. I kept expecting the moment where I'd finally feel caught up, and it never arrived, because "caught up" was never a real place. It was just the horizon moving with me.
What actually broke the loop wasn't a big realization. It was noticing how I felt after posting something online that did well. For a few hours I'd feel sharp, ahead of the curve, like I understood something other people didn't. Then a day later I'd open the code I was supposedly writing about and realize I hadn't gone any deeper on it. The post made me feel smarter than I was. It didn't make me smarter. Those are different things, and I had quietly let the first one substitute for the second for way too long.
That was the trap I had to name out loud before I could get out of it. Talking about engineering had become easier and more rewarding, in the short term, than doing engineering. Writing a thread about a concept gave me faster feedback than sitting with the concept until I understood it well enough to actually break it down. So I kept choosing the thread. Not because I decided to, but because the loop was built to pull me there, and I never stopped to check whether it was pulling me somewhere useful.
So I changed what I was optimizing for. Instead of asking "does this make me look ahead," I started asking "does this make me better." Those two questions have almost nothing to do with each other, and most of my old habits only survived because I'd never separated them. An internship that looks great on a resume might teach you very little. A weekend spent actually debugging something painful, with no audience and no post at the end of it, might teach you everything.
The shift wasn't dramatic. I didn't quit anything publicly or announce a new era. I just started spending more hours with my own projects and fewer hours narrating them. I stopped treating every process, every interview loop, every opportunity as a referendum on whether I was good enough, and started treating my own growth as the only scoreboard that actually matters, because it's the only one still there after the opportunity ends.
Which is what I'm actually trying to do this year. Work more in silence. Not secretive, just quieter. Build things and let the learning happen inside the building instead of in a caption about the building. Do more of my own research, the slow kind that doesn't produce a shareable result every week. And take the startup effort I care about and actually work on it, on my own, low key, through research and building instead of through updates. If it turns into something, it'll be because the work was real, not because I announced it early enough times.
None of this means stop preparing for the future entirely. It means I stopped treating "staying ahead" as the goal and started treating it as a side effect of doing good work consistently, which it always should have been.
A few things that actually helped, if you recognize any of this in yourself:
- Separate the feeling of progress from actual progress. If something makes you feel smart fast, check whether it made you better slowly.
- Ask what you're optimizing for before saying yes to the next opportunity. "Does this help me grow" and "does this look good" are different questions with different answers.
- Let some work stay private. Not everything needs an audience to be worth doing, and some things get worse when you narrate them too early.
- Pick your own pace instead of someone else's path. Copying a trajectory you admire will always leave you one step behind it.
- Treat quiet stretches as normal, not as falling behind. Real building has long stretches with nothing to show for it yet.
preview: For a while I thought staying ahead meant chasing every opportunity in sight. It just left me tired and never satisfied.

title: Breaking Down the Monolith in the Middle of a Transplant Match
content:
The team I am on sits in the middle of international donor transplant work. A patient is on one side, a donor is on the other, often in a different country, and we move the data between them. We handle the matching, the allocation, and the rendering of that data, and we support the federal contracts that come with it. That last part means getting the required data to the right government for wherever the transplant happens, whether that is Buenos Aires or Flint, Michigan.
Most of that orchestration runs through a legacy C# monolith. It is not broken. It is not down. It is just slow enough to matter, and when the thing moving through the pipe decides whether someone gets a transplant, slow enough to matter is the only bar that counts.
## What I am actually working on
My piece is breaking that monolith down and moving toward microservices. Not because microservices are fashionable, but because the monolith makes every part of the pipeline move at the speed of its slowest section. Splitting it lets matching, allocation, and delivery scale on their own terms and fail on their own terms.
Alongside that, we are looking at how tightly we can compact the data and how fast we can move it. The target is millisecond-level transfer that holds up under failure: fault tolerant, scalable, and reliable when a node or a region goes away.
## Why this one feels different
I have spent the last five or six months reading system design more or less continuously. Queues, partitioning, replication, what happens when a message is sent and never received. Most of that was theory I was collecting without anywhere to put it.
This is where it goes. The questions I was working through on paper are the same questions in the ticket queue now, except the answer has a patient attached to it. That is a good reason to get it right.
preview: My team moves international donor transplant data between patient and donor, and a legacy C# monolith sits in the middle of it. Here is what breaking that apart into microservices looks like, and why millisecond-level transfer is the bar.
